text: I am currently serving in my first term as the Deputy President of the Singapore Dragonboat Association, together with hon Member Mr Alex Yeo and was formerly a National Youth Athlete in ten-pin bowling under the National Youth Development Programme.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I was a beneficiary of the original Sports Excellence 2000 scheme.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Although I left competitive bowling more than two decades ago, I have watched, with great interest, how Singapore sports have evolved since then and our laudable approach in harnessing the potential of our local talents.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In the sport of ten-pin bowling, our young bowlers have gone on to win world championships and broadly, our athletes now train with more structured pathways.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: More importantly, our sporting ecosystem has grown to support not just elite performance, but also inclusion and participation across the community.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For example, I understand that there are at least nine para inclusive teams in the dragon-boating community with an estimated 250 para athletes who might be physically or intellectually impaired.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I have seen first-hand the discipline and commitment required of all athletes, the importance of strong governance and access to facilities and the impact of initiatives that broaden opportunity – all of which are directly supported and reinforced by the reforms in this Bill.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The amendments to the Singapore Sports Council Act updates our legislative framework to better reflect the current sporting environment in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They clarify the role of Sport Singapore, strengthen governance and recognise a wider range of sporting activities, while continuing to support both high performance sport and mass participation.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mind sports, such as chess and bridge are internationally governed with their international federations recognised by the International Olympic Committee.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These disciplines have also featured as medal events in major multi-sport competitions, including the Asian Games.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: E-sports have similarly developed into structured and regulated competitive activities.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They were included as official medal events at the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou and most recently at the 2025 SEA Games.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At the elite level, competitors in mind sports and e-sports undergo systematic training, compete under sustained pressure and commit years to preparation and performance.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: These characteristics are consistent with what we already recognise in high performance sport.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Many athletes continue to train over long periods, often while balancing work or study and have to rely on a stable and well-governed sporting ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This Bill preserves the statutory framework that enables that support.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: By recognising a broader range of sporting activities, the Bill allows our policies to remain relevant to evolving participation patterns, while continuing to uphold high standards of sporting integrity and excellence.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Bill strengthens SportSG's mandate to establish and uphold standards across coaching, equipment, facilities and accreditation.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In doing so, it reinforces a clear principle: high standards are not optional in sport, they are foundational.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is particularly important in Singapore's context, where most athletes are not full-time professionals.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For many, sport is pursued alongside education or employment.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Our system must therefore support not just peak performance, but the whole athlete and the full sporting journey, including welfare, career pathways and transitions beyond competitive sport, recognising that only a small proportion remain in high performance sport for life.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Bill also reinforces SportSG's role in promoting physical activity across the population.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: With a super aged society in Singapore, physical activity is no longer only a sporting issue, it is a public health imperative.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Regular activity supports physical health, mental well-being and independence among seniors.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: By strengthening SportSG's mandate, we invest not only in sport, but in healthier ageing and a more resilient society.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Singapore first competed at the Paralympic Games in the 1980s and our Paralympians won their first medals at the 2008 Beijing Paralympics.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Since then, they have continued to represent Singapore with distinction at subsequent Games.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Their achievements remind us that sporting excellence is not defined by ability, but by determination and by performance.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Singapore National Paralympic Council plays a critical role in supporting these athletes from development pathways to high performance preparation.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: By affirming this partnership in statute, the Bill reinforces a fundamental principle – that access to opportunity, support and excellence in sport should be open to all who have the commitment to pursue it.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But Mr Speaker, I do have a few clarifications to make.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In a public body with such influence, how members are chosen is not just administrative – it is a question of integrity, trust and accountability.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Specifically, given challenges unique to Singapore's sporting landscape, including the realities faced by non-full-time athletes and gaps in support for certain sports, how will the Council's composition address these issues?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Will experience from countries facing similar constraints be considered?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A Council that reflects these realities will be one that can make fair, informed and relevant decisions.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The increase in membership numbers can then be justified.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They hail from sports, such as fencing, swimming, shooting, wushu and silat – truly deserving athletes who exemplify dedication and excellence.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: However, I would like to ask how scholars are chosen.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: How the Government determines the number of scholarships each year and whether athletes in mind sports and e-sports will be considered in the future?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Will there be a clear, publicly available framework explaining how criteria are applied?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Transparency here is not optional; it empowers athletes to plan their careers and chase excellence with confidence.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Lastly, on making sports facilities accessible to all.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Given SportSG's expanded role, clear guidelines and fair processes are essential.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Access to facilities must be a right, not a privilege.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In my line of work, I have seen how the Government pragmatically allows vacant industrial land under JTC to be leased out on a short-term basis for solar energy generation.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This ensures land does not sit idle while still retaining long-term planning flexibility.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: That same principle can and should be applied to sports.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Temporarily unused open spaces can be leased to sports organisations and community groups to create facilities for training, grassroots programmes and competitions.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This not only maximises land use efficiency, but also lowers barriers to participation, supports community sport and allows SportSG to meet demand without waiting for a permanent infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Efficient access strengthens trust, encourages participation and ensures our sporting ecosystem works for everyone in the country.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And notwithstanding these questions, I support the Bill, because it strengthens SportSG, supports our athletes and ensures opportunities for sporting excellence are truly open to all in a country.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And to put on record, I thank Team Singapore for showing us what resilience looks like, because these athletes do not need a wake-up call.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They have been answering the call of duty every single day.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I join many hon Members of this House, appreciating our sporting talents, particularly for the strong showing at the SEA Games, as well as the Asian Youth Para Games, where athletes showed impressive debuts.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Much like the hon Member Kenneth Goh, I tag key pivotal moments to memories.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I remembered Joseph Schooling winning the first ever gold medal for Singapore in Olympics.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I was at the newsroom, and like the rest of my colleagues, holding our breaths.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Similarly, this year, when Diyanah Aqidah and Nicholas Khaw won Singapore's first gold of the season in taekwondo, no less after a drought, I remembered being at a healthcare institution visiting a patient who also rejoiced when the app alert came in.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Similarly, when our 12-year-old athlete won a medal in sailing, and this was Anya Zahedi, I remembered being at a community event where grassroots leaders also rejoiced when receiving the notification that such a young sporting talent was able to achieve significant success in a sporting arena.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Continuing down memory lane, like most Singaporeans, my core memories of school, for the learning journeys or excursions and of awesome Physical Education classes where we were introduced to new sport.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: In primary school, I learned to swim and was inspired by swim queen Joscelin.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: In secondary school, we played heaps of captain's and netball, inspired by the Vandas.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: And in my tertiary years, enjoyed rugby – always looking forward to the Sevens.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The competitive nature of sports is a longstanding one.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: However, beyond competition and sportsmanship, sports can also bridge communities, through shared experiences, as Singaporeans bond over a mutual love for a good game – football, cycling and pickleball.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: In order for sports to continue strengthening our social cohesion, we should ensure sport is accessible to all Singaporeans beyond a privileged few, as the hon Dr Hamid has mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: We should also ensure sport is accessible early, to young children and to persons with disabilities.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Sports should not be the new measure of affluence.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Beyond recreation, Singapore should also continue in our pursuit to ensure stronger support for our athletes and sporting organisations to help them succeed as they fly our flag proudly.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: This Bill must be poised to take sports in Singapore to the next chapter, and it has my support.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I am hopeful that the Bill will lower barrier to access and inclusivity in sports, ensure a balance of excelling in physical, mind and e-sports, as well as ensure holistic education and career support to young as well as professional athletes.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It also underscored the importance of partnerships in building a robust and inclusive ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I am hopeful for Singapore to see an increase in the number of inclusive sporting facilities and skilled coaches who are attuned and also trained to the needs of our para-athletes, equipping them to empower themselves through sports.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Some athletes I spoke to, some para-athletes, in particular, are hopeful for increased resources including scholarships or funds to draw upon in their sporting journey.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: While recognition kickstarts the institutionalisation of mind sports, there must continue to be support for its growth.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: E-sports organisations and its stakeholders should also be able to expand their capabilities, organise training sessions and tournaments to be able to assess confidently as well as enhance the abilities of athletes.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: E-sports, such as chess and bridge, present a unique opportunity for Singaporeans to engage with one another regardless of age or physical abilities.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It is important to continue creating a positive and healthy environment to support the participation and training of Singaporean athletes by ensuring competence of coaches.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It is also, however, equally important to ensure that e-sport and mind sport does not quite replace but compliments physical sport choices.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Additionally, the amendments will empower SportSG to establish institutions to develop and train national athletes, overseeing their sporting and academic pathways, expanding their versions of success.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The SSP will retain its identity as a school while strengthening its role as the education arm of high-performance sport systems.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: In September, I raised a Parliamentary Question (PQ) to ask on support for youth athletes juggling sporting and academic commitments.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It is not an easy feat and I hope SportSG will continue to consider providing greater support for the holistic development of young athletes, many of whom are already facing high pressure situations and societal expectations.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I believe it is important for the Government to recognise, appreciate and better support our child and young athletes and their families.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I recently met with A, a dedicated father who discovered sport as a coping mechanism for his first son.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: While the family sent, in Cantonese, "Kor Kor", for badminton coaching, they also discovered that their second son has potential, especially as he has been watching "Kor Kor" train on the sidelines.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: A shared with me that the family made a decision to get his second son to also start training early, since around preschool.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: With proper guidance, the second son was able to play confidently in matches beyond his age category.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Investing in developing sporting expertise from a very young age is a long and costly journey.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Speaker, the profiles of our sporting talents are varied.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: One Fengshan resident, E, is a mom of one.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: She is also a professional boxer, representing Singapore in international matches.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: (In Malay): Sports brings people together even if they have different views or support the opposing team.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Sports can also transform lives and represent an opportunity that should ideally be accessible to all segments of society and not exclusive.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For sports to continue strengthening our social cohesion, we should ensure that sport is not merely confined to a selected few.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I recently met a resident, Mr A, a father who shared his challenges in supporting his children's badminton training expenses since preschool.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: He mentioned that several other parents share the hope that Singapore can encourage and support them, so that sporting talents can be spotted earlier and this will help develop budding athletes at an early age.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: (In English): Speaker, in gist, the intention of this Bill is to strengthen inclusivity, expand participation and provide better support for athletes of all forms.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I therefore call on MCCY as well as the private sector to lend their support and do their best to ensure sport organisations have sufficient resources to support the ambitions and performance of our athletes, and to forge new partnerships with each other to ensure sports always remain relevant and accessible and also meaningful for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The Singapore Sports Council was set up in 1973 and renamed as Sport Singapore in 2014.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The local sporting landscape has grown significantly and become more vibrant, especially over the past decade.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The sporting ecosystem has also become more holistic and well-resourced.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Our national athletes are flying our Singapore flag high, with more podium finishes in the Olympics and other Major Games and world championships in recent years.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Across different parts of Singapore, there are high quality recreational sports facilities, such as ActiveSG sports stadiums, swimming pools, gyms and world-class competition venues, such as the OCBC Aquatic Centre.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There is the MyActiveSG+ platform to book and use these facilities conveniently and affordably.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Indeed, we have much going on for us in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This is a landscape populated by a whole community of sports administrators, coaches, athletes, guided by the vision to Live Better Through Sport, a vision set for Singapore sports for 2030.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Singapore sports is growing in ambition and reach.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: As part of the Kallang Alive Masterplan, the Singapore Sports School in Woodlands will shift to The Kallang.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Sports tourism in Singapore is also experiencing a boom as more international sporting events are held here.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: For instance, the Standard Chartered Marathon, Singapore Rugby Sevens and the World Table Tennis Singapore Smash are some of the world-class sporting events that have attracted sports fans and their families to Singapore every year.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: To realise Vision 2030 and live out the goals set for The Kallang Masterplan, there is indeed a need for deeper expertise and experience to develop the new specialised functions, such as precinct and infrastructure development, international sports events organisation as well as sports education and professional skills development.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Moreover, significant Government funding for these infrastructure development and programme development will be required.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Therefore, strong leadership and governance from the Sport Singapore Board is critical to ensure taxpayers' contributions allocated for sports development are not for an idealistic dream but is well-spent and will uplift our entire nation towards achieving better lives through sports.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The Sport Singapore Board will play a crucial role in this transformation journey.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: As with any Board, its duties include ensuring strong governance, management, accountability and alignment with key sporting goals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I, therefore, agree with the amendment to increase the Board from 15 to 25 members.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The current Sport Singapore Board has a bench strength of 15 members and comprises members from the private, public sectors as well as national sports associations and athletes, directly appointed by the Minister for Community, Culture and Youth.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In the current Sport Singapore Board composition, seven out of 15 members have a finance-related professional background.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Only one member is from a National Sports Association, one member from the Singapore National Olympic Council and one member is a Paralympian.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I would suggest that with 10 additional Board seats, the Board members should have a greater diversity of professional backgrounds and would, in turn, bring to the table wider industry networks.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: For instance, professionals or experts in sports education, sports psychology, sports tourism, community sports and senior sports would bring valuable insights and perspectives into technical capability building, community sports programming and sports excellence for the elite athletes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Aside from looking at the number of members alone, we might also introduce other measures, such as term limits, which is good practice in the spirit of renewal.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I recall that one previous Board Chairman had served 16 years.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Last, when it comes to Board seats, it is not merely a numbers game but one of commitment, interest, expertise and passion.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: With more Board members bringing a wider breath of experience and networks as well as deeper expertise, SportSG is well placed to bring sports in Singapore to new and greater heights.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I would also like to pose a challenge to the better-resourced SportSG board, to aim for a more aspirational vision.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Beyond improving the lives of individuals, sports can also uplift and bond the entire nation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In October 2021, I spoke in this House on how sports can bond Singaporeans together.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Sports can strengthen our bodies and minds, toughen our fighting spirit and uplift our spirits during difficult times.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Sports can also bring Singaporeans of different races and religions, socio-economic backgrounds together and be the unifying force that bonds and builds Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In the recent 33rd SEA Games in Thailand, Singapore sent the largest ever contingent of 930 athletes across 48 sports.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I know how hard our athletes trained, the sacrifices they made and how hard they fought for every point.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Each time the Singapore flag is raised and Majulah Singapura is sung, I felt immensely proud of what our young athletes have achieved.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I also met many Team Nila supporters, more than 200 of them who took time to travel to Thailand in support of our athletes competing in various sports.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I also know of many Singaporeans back home who were glued to MeWatch, following the competitions and cheering for our athletes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There were many inspiring moments that stole our hearts, seeing how our young athletes fought against their competitors to fly our Singaporean flag high.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Many would remember how fencer, Amita Berthier, made a spectacular consecutive seven-point comeback to claim victory over her opponent and eventually claimed her third title in Women's Individual Foil event.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There was also 14-year-old swimmer Julia Yeo and her gungho can-do spirit.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Julia is a symbol of all that sports can do – physical and mental strength, a spirit of overcoming and a pride and commitment to the process.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: This Singapore spirit will be the most precious achievement, more than any number of gold medals.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I think we definitely should appreciate all of them and I would like to thank them.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This Bill recognises something many Singaporeans already know from lived experience – that the way we engage through sport has evolved.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And our laws need to evolve with it.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But as we widen definitions and expand powers, it is worth pausing to ask not just what we enable, but how these changes will affect people differently – especially our youths, families with fewer resources, and athletes who are already under pressure.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: As a psychologist, I see sport not only as physical activity or competition, but as part of a wider social system.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When designed thoughtfully, it builds confidence, resilience and belonging.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When it is not, it can unintentionally add stress and widen gaps.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I support the inclusion of mind sports and e-sports in our legal framework.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Chess, bridge and competitive gaming have grown significantly in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Many young people already invest time, effort and identity in these activities.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Recognising them signals that we acknowledge different forms of talent, including those based on cognitive skills.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: At the same time, recognition also carries responsibility.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: By defining e-sports as "sports" as sports, we are not just enabling support – we are shaping norms.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We are signalling what is legitimate and encouraged.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: And that is why the conditions around recognition matter.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Many youths I meet are motivated and capable, but also increasingly tired.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: They spend long hours on screens – often alone, often under pressure – to perform, to rank and sometimes to secure opportunities like Direct School Admission (DSA).

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This reflects a growing imbalance in how technology fits into young people's lives.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: As SportSG extends support into this space, it would be useful to hear how governance frameworks will evolve to ensure that youth protection and athlete welfare remain central.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: For publicly supported programmes, it would be helpful to have clear expectations – around training hours, physical conditioning, sleep and posture education, and referral pathways when concerning behaviours emerge.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: These are not meant to restrict interest, but to protect well-being.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: There is also a governance dimension we should consider.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Unlike traditional sports, e-sports are not governed by independent federations.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: They are owned by private publishers, who control game rules, competition formats and even when a title continues to exist.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: International research cautions that governance models dominated by commercial interests may not always align with public interest goals – particularly when it comes to athlete welfare, integrity and transparency.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Next, the expanded definition of sport also has implications for education.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Sports-based DSA pathways have opened doors for many students.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But families with more resources are often better positioned to invest in coaching, equipment, or overseas exposure.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It is important that these pathways support balanced development, rather than a narrow focus at a young age.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: More broadly, inequality in sport often starts much earlier than we realise.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Some families have the means and confidence to take risks.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Others worry about what happens if their child invests heavily in sport but has limited options later on.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: That is why I strongly support the Bill's provision for educational and career support for both active and retired sportspersons.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: It helps reduce the sense that pursuing sport is an all-or-nothing decision.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: But I would also ask whether we have sufficient early-stage, school- and community-based systems to identify and support talented youths from lower-resource families before gaps widen.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: If sport development is meant to start early, then access and reassurance for families need to start early too.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: These concerns are made more pressing by the reality that national sports funding is already constrained.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: NSAs compete for funding based on alignment with Vision 2030, key performance indicators, governance standards and development plans.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Athletes in traditional sports have raised concerns about gaps in institutional support, particularly beyond the top tier.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: While recognising mind sports and e-sports, we should remain clear that physical activity remains central to public health.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Resilience is built not only through mental effort, but through movement, teamwork and learning how to recover from setbacks.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: I therefore welcome the Bill's explicit expansion of SportSG's role in promoting physical fitness activities.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: At the same time, smaller volunteer-led groups may worry about capacity.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Elite athletes face significant pressure and uncertainty, especially as they transition out of competitive sport.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We should support athletes not only at their peak, but through the transitions that follow.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: These indicators matter if we want to support athletes as people, not just performers.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This Bill gives SportSG greater flexibility – and with it, greater responsibility.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: With careful implementation, attention to equity and safeguards for youth well-being, these amendments can strengthen a sporting ecosystem that supports Singaporeans across different abilities, backgrounds and stages of life.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At its heart, this Bill is a modernisation exercise.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I support these changes because it also recognises three realities.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Competition today not only happens on courts and tracks, but also on boards and screens.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Some of our young people compete in inter-school chess championships, while others represent their campus in organised e-sports tournaments.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is no longer just about participation in sport, but building an active, preventive-health culture.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Physical activity is increasingly seen as an upstream investment in long-term health and well-being.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, high performance sport today is scientific and multidisciplinary.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The Bill emphasises on standards, accreditation and institutions that reflects this reality.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: While I support the Bill, I would raise four clusters of issues for consideration on mind sports, e-sports, broader system implications and active living through physical fitness and the built environment.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My first set of questions, like many have spoken, relates to the meaning and operationalisation of the term "mind sports".

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My question is: how will SportSG operationalise recognition of mind sports beyond the examples in the Bill?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Specifically, are there any tangible inclusion and/or exclusion criteria that can be laid out?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For instance, in my view, mind sports typically consist of one, or a combination of the following: deep concentration, memory, pattern recognition, decision-making under time pressure and composure under stress.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But these characteristics are not unique to chess or bridge alone.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In my conversations with my residents and also my volunteers after Meet-the-People Sessions, they asked, "David, would games like Pokemon cards, mahjong, poker also be considered as mind sports?" because if those characteristics I mentioned earlier, they do qualify.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I must tell you one that someone mentioned.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They asked, "Would even buying Toto or 4D at Singapore Pools outlet could be construed as some as a form of mind sport because there is some element of competition in winning a few million dollars?" Some may even say, "It involves some level of intellect because you have to study the number pattern that have "opened" previously before you decide what number to buy." So, without clear criteria, we may risk inconsistent decisions, disputes and perception that mind sports is ad hoc.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We know from research that competitive e-sports training can be intense.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: One recent academic paper summarised that e-sports athletes may train four to 10 hours per day.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For a minority, gaming can become especially problematic given its addictive potential.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In this context, I welcome that the Bill because it strengthens SportSG's ability to set codes of practice, guidelines and accreditation standards.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These powers are important in e-sports, where quality and safeguards vary widely today.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In this respect, I have three questions on how these powers might be used well.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This could encompass age-appropriate guidelines on training hours, mandatory breaks, expectations around sleep hygiene, because that is what parents tell, and a required physical conditioning component.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: That aim here is not about micromanaging, but it is about building healthy norms, especially for under-18s who are immersed in the world of e-sports.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Second, will SportSG require accreditation for e-sports coaches and training centres that run structured programmes for our youths?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If e-sports is to be treated as a sport, then coaching should also be treated as a profession, with standards and safeguarding expectations, and clear escalation pathways.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, will SportSG consider proactively working with relevant agencies from the start to develop parent-facing guidance, for instance, with MOE and the Ministry of Social Development and Family?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Presently, many parents tell me that they struggle to distinguish between training from play, or even to assess readiness of their child to take part in competitive e-sports.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A national framework and research-driven guidance could help parents to understand signs of readiness, set healthy boundaries, recognise warning signs of addiction, such as sleep disruption, mood changes or social withdrawal.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We should also give thought to seek consent from parents whose children are under-18 entering higher-commitment e-sports pathways, so that parents know what is the child enrolling into and can provide the requisite support.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My third point pertains to broader systemic concerns arising from this Bill.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Second, recognition should not blur an important distinction.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Mind sports and e-sports are not interchangeable with physical sports.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We have made a deliberate and forward-looking policy choice to adopt a broader legal definition of sport.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But we must be equally deliberate in our messaging that physical activity remains irreplaceable for health, development and lifelong functioning.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Mind sports and e-sports build cognition, community and excellence, but they cannot substitute movement.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: An active mind should sit alongside an active body.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, there are downstream implications, particularly for schools.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Today, activities like chess are often treated as clubs rather than sports co-curricular activities (CCAs).

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: With this Bill, students, parents and educators may ask whether this should change, that should not be a club but will be now seen as a sport.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Where interest exists, schools should know how activities can be supported, coached and how participation is valued.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Relatedly, how might this affect pathways, such as entry into the SSP?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If not, are there parallel alternative pathways that exist for students who demonstrate excellence in mind sports or e-sports to develop and compete internationally?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This aligns well with our national shift toward preventive health.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My question is when the Bill speaks about "planning" and "promotion", does it extend beyond programmes into shaping the everyday Built environment that makes such activity easier or harder?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For instance, when someone engages in a physical sport, it does depend on the facilities or infrastructure, whether it is available or accessible near home.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If such options are far from home, poorly connected or inconvenient to access, the best campaigns will still struggle to translate into daily practice or adoption.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I previously asked the Minister for National Development in Parliament about the feasibility of converting Housing and Development Board (HDB) car park spaces for alternative uses for sports or recreational spaces.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In the written reply, the Minister explained that HDB must take into account of parking demand over time, potential disamenities to residents, technical and safety constraints, such as fire safety provisions, exit capacity and structural loading.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The reply also noted that where suitable, HDB has supported such requests by converting upper levels of the multi-storey car parks to greenery and community gardens, and HDB will consider other community-benefiting uses subject to site-specific assessment.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I appreciate the need for safety and site-specific assessment.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, the current posture could feel a little reactive.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, both physical sports and mind sports, such as chess can stand to benefit from the conversion of such spaces.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They could start modestly as pilots with clear safety and feasibility criteria, and the designs that are low-cost, low-disamenity and easy to maintain.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Such a proactive approach would help turning "planning and promotion" into something that residents can feel in their daily lives: more convenient spaces to move, closer to home, built into the rhythm into their neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In particular, I support the recognition of mind sports and e-sports because it acknowledges that excellence can be achieved cognitively and also physically because recognition can bring structure, standards and safety.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But at the same time, we must pair recognition with clear guardrails and clear messaging.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Mind sports and e-sports should complement, not replace, physical activity, which remains foundational for health and well-being.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And as we pursue preventive health, I hope we can look creatively into under-utilised spaces that can support active living in our neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding, I have several clarifications on how these expanded powers will translate into everyday outcomes for residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mr, Speaker, Sir, my first clarification concerns everyday access, affordability and the quality of sports facilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As we expand Sport Singapore's (SportSG's) functions under clause 6(a), we must be clear that success is measured by active living, not just by walking to the bus stop.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the broadened mandate under clauses 6(e) and (f) to manage facilities, how will this translate into our estates?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will SportSG prioritise less visible but high-impact infrastructure such as community gyms within a 10-minute walk of neighbourhood blocks over marquee facilities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Residents also ask a basic question: will they be able to play sports to their heart's content?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, securing a court often feels like winning the lottery.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We also see rising social friction such as noise disputes involving pickleball.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These conflicts indicate that our infrastructure may be struggling to keep pace with trends.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If SportSG is to manage facilities under clause 6(e), how will design standards such as acoustic mitigation and smarter space planning be strengthened so that sports bind the community rather than create tension?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must also ensure that we are not designing this Bill only for the active majority.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without deliberate intervention, expanded powers may simply help the fit get fitter while the inactive remain behind due to cost or constraints.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This leads to the financial powers in clauses 7(b) and (c), allowing grants and loans to individuals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, how will SportSG ensure funds reach small heartland operators?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is a risk that grants flow to large well-resourced organisations while the void deck taekwondo club or the Zumba interest group is deprioritised.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If SportSG must do more with the same resources, the Minister must clarify what will be deprioritised.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure that these new regulatory ambitions do not come at the expense of core maintenance and grassroots programmes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clauses 6(m) and (n) empower SportSG to establish codes of practice and accredit coaches and facilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Residents want safety, well-maintained equipment and qualified coaches.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, accreditation can become a barrier to entry.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will these powers inadvertently create a "pay-to-play" system?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If freelance instructors and community groups cannot afford the time or cost to navigate accreditation, they may be priced out.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must avoid over-professionalising the sector to the point where affordable community-level coaching disappears.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Codes under clause 6(m) work for mainstream sports but may stifle organic activities like parkour, street dance or informal seniors' exercises.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I ask the Minister to assure the House that we will not regulate these activities out of existence simply because they do not fit into an accreditation box.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a progressive step that validates the aspirations of our youths.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, as a member of the People's Action Party (PAP) Mental Health Group, I sound a note of caution.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Recognition gives credibility to a dream, but it can also become an excuse.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Parents already grapple with excessive screen time, only to be told by their children, "I am not addicted, I am training to go pro." The glamour of professional e-sports masks the truth that only a tiny fraction make it while many risk addiction, sleep disruption and neglected studies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we legitimise e-sports, we must legitimise the safety framework around it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, given that e-sports ecosystems are tied to betting and aggressive sponsorship, why does the Bill not include explicit safeguards for minors alongside the expanded accreditation powers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must also address the "cliff edge" of an e-sports career.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Is there a plan for youths who do not reach the top tier?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Career and education support must be core, not peripheral.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be plans for aspiring e-sports athletes to be admitted into our Sports School so that academic development progresses in tandem with sporting development?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we recognise the sport, we must protect the athlete.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I welcome clause 6(b), which names the Singapore National Paralympic Council as a key partner.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But naming a partner is not legislating outcomes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Significant barriers remain in transport and facility access.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will facilities managed under clause 6(e) be subject to accessibility standards beyond basic building codes?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To do this, we need disaggregated data by disability type, age and town.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This strengthens elite development but raises questions about equity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Without clear criteria and financial safeguards, will these institutions favour families who can afford intensive training?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many national athletes currently juggle fulltime studies or work while competing against fulltime international rivals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must not build systems that assume athletes can absorb personal financial strain indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we expect high performance, we must be honest about whether current support is adequate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Beyond money, we must measure success beyond medals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can I book a court without fighting for it?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can my child learn safely without paying a premium?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can my parents stay active with dignity, not obstacles?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can a young person chase a sporting dream on a track or on a screen without falling off a cliff when the dream ends?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These questions run through the points I have raised today: access to neighbourhood facilities, fair funding for heartland groups, safety without excessive cost, responsible recognition of e-sports, meaningful inclusion for seniors and persons with disabilities, and training pathways that support athletes not just to compete, but to live well beyond sports.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I say this as someone shaped by sports.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As a former competitive gymnast, canoeist and dragon boater, I learnt that sports does not just train the body, it trains the spirit.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It teaches us how to fall and how to stand up again.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It teaches us that progress is never an individual act.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a relay and we run our leg so the next person can run theirs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The purpose of this House is not to pass laws that look good in print, but to pass laws that work – in parks, in void decks, in schools, in community clubs and in the homes where parents are raising resilient children.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We saw this clearly in the recently concluded Southeast Asian Games (SEA Games).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We rightly celebrate our athletes' achievements and medal haul.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Once again, we also saw the immense sacrifices made by Singaporeans who train while studying, working and supporting families, often competing against fulltime athletes from other countries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Their performances should make us proud but should also prompt us to reflect on whether our systems are truly designed to support sustained excellence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, let us be ambitious but also be honest.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us build the flagship facilities, yes, but also the quiet corners of fitness that keep a nation healthy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us professionalise where needed but never price out the heartland.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Let us pursue excellence, but refuse to leave behind the inactive, the vulnerable, the senior, the person with disability or the young person who does not make it to the top.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We will build a stronger Singapore in everyday life.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The amendments before us expand SportSG's remit in ways that reflect how Singaporeans actually engage with sport today.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Bill's inclusion of mind sports and e-sports in our definition of sports signals that Singapore recognises competitive excellence wherever it emerges.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill also empowers SportSG to establish institutions for elite athlete development, to accredit coaches and facilities, and to support athletes beyond their competitive years.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are practical expansions that will strengthen our sporting ecosystem from grassroots to podium.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as we broaden SportSG's mandate, we must also sharpen our oversight.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Expansion without accountability risks diluting impact and eroding public trust.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I raise four areas for greater clarity.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill grants SportSG authority to establish institutions for developing and training sportspersons.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Entities like the Singapore Sports School and the Singapore Sport Institute have been nurturing athletes for years.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The consolidation of these institutions, announced earlier this year, is happening alongside this legislative change.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Building on the Auditor-General's Office's constructive observations in its recent report regarding procurement, grant management and revenue contracting, we have an opportunity to establish clear governance frameworks that will serve SportSG well as it takes on new responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Strong institutional safeguards now will protect both athletes and public trust as the organisation evolves.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When we task institutions with the holistic development of young athletes, overseeing not just their training but also their academic curricula and well-being, we are asking them to act in loco parentis.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Safe Sport framework exists and the Safe Sport Commission has made progress since its launch.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will their performance indicators, safeguarding records and funding utilisation be reported to this House annually?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, on eligibility and support for e-sports and mind sports athletes.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill expands the definition of sports to include mind sports and e-sports.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What matters is whether athletes in these disciplines will have the same access to funding, facilities and national representation pathways as their counterparts in athletics or football.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Singapore Esports Association has announced plans for a national training centre.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Just over the weekend, we launched an e-sports hub in Bishan Community Centre that is purpose-built for seniors.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps one day we might field an inter-generational team to represent Singapore in our community in e-sports competitions!

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there long-term plans for mind sports and e-sports associations to receive the same level of institutional support as National Sports Associations (NSAs) in traditional sports?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill grants SportSG new powers to establish codes of practice for coaching, training, equipment and facilities – and to accredit or certify compliance with those standards.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a regulatory function, not just a developmental one.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What mechanisms will ensure transparency and accountability in the issuance of coaching accreditations, facility certifications and training programme approvals under the amended Act?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will there be independent review panels for contested decisions?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will accreditation criteria and outcomes be published annually?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Lastly, this Bill also expands SportsSG's remit with regard to planning and promoting physical fitness activities alongside sports, fostering research into physical fitness and establishing codes of practice, guidelines and standards for wider coaching, training and equipment.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are there plans to dovetail initiatives or align longer-term policy changes where there are overlaps in governmental remit?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Competitive sport forges excellence and resilience in our athletes while anchoring Singapore's global reputation; we cannot be a thriving nation without champions.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Recently, I the privilege of meeting our SEA Games medalist Isaiah Tang, who started karate lessons in Bishan Community Centre (CC) when he was just seven years old.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In his debut at last year's SEA Games Isaiah came back with a bronze medal.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I was greatly touched when he asked about what young athletes like him needed.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He did not share immediately about funding or recognition but shared instead about opportunities and exposure to competitions.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He is the archetype of a home-grown champion that we as a nation should be proud of.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: All the same, support is instrumental for the growth, maturity and further development of home-grown talents like Isaiah.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He shared that his family flew up to Thailand to cheer him on at the most recent SEA Games.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More than just family support, however, our talent requires the resources and opportunities that institutional support brings.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Bill is a large step in the right direction, to further build up the kampung of support around our natural home-grown athletes and champions; but there is still space to grow.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When we invest in sport, we invest in the kind of country we want to be.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If you want to go far, go together in a team".

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But today, I want just to add on "If you want to go even further, go together in a bigger team".

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: That is exactly how the Prime Minister described for the "we first" society – we need a village to raise an athlete.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In my time as a gymnast in 1980s, we had no professional coaches, no professional facilities, needless to say no specialised equipment like today.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As schoolmates, we trained one another, learning from books and sheer determination.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I vividly remember my first SEA Games in 1985.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We were required to compete in six apparatus, one of the apparatuses is Roman Rings, yet we did not even have the proper equipment to train on.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We practised on metal rings instead of the laminated wood.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We set up the rings under the blazing sun to train because we did not have a high ceiling hall.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Sometimes, the metal rings were so hot causing our palms to burn.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And we resorted to training in the night and bear in mind, not much light.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Needless to say, when there is rain, we cannot even train.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Even the training hours, without scientific, we have to train every day from 2.00 pm to 11.00 pm after school.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Saturday, Sunday, we train from 8.00 am to 2.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: That was the reality of being an athlete 40 years ago, driven not by comfort or resources but by passion, resilience and an unwavering commitment to represent Singapore with pride.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This amendment makes our sports policy framework more comprehensive and better able to address Singapore's future sporting needs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It not only updates the system, but also better reflects how Singaporeans participate in sports, responding to the lifestyle habits and needs of different age groups.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When I was young, I was a national gymnast.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: On the gymnastics floor, I learnt not just techniques, but focus, discipline and sportsmanship and these values have stayed with me to this day, benefiting me for life.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I still remember the moments of falling down again and again during training, then getting back up and the encouragement and interaction between teammates.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The unwavering strength to "take a step forward" is what sports gave me.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Today, when I see residents of different generations exercising at community clubs, neighbourhood parks and schools, I am reminded of the values that sports bring us.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Sports make communities more vibrant and the spirit that sports convey transcends time, age and background.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This amendment is to ensure this lifestyle receives better support, a safer environment and a more sustainable direction for development.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In our communities, elderly people play chess, young people are passionate about e-sports and children try new physical activities.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The forms are different, but they all require strategy, focus and endurance and can also cultivate team spirit.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Including these activities in the definition of "sport" allows the Sports Council to more systematically and purposefully support and manage these developments, ensuring they grow on a healthy and safe trajectory.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This also reminds us that the value of sports should not be measured only in traditional ways.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As long as the direction is right, mind sports and e-sports can, like traditional sports, help participants build confidence, discipline and team spirit.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: More residents are participating in physical activities such as yoga, strength training, fitness classes and running.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These activities improve physical and mental health and also create more interaction between neighbours.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Including physical activities in the Council's responsibilities means the Government recognises the public value of these activities and provides a clearer framework for promoting community fitness programmes in the future.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This will further promote a culture of "Active together", making exercise a lifestyle that more residents can easily and sustainably participate in.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Regardless of which sport they participate in, residents should be active in safe and reliable environments.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Establishing standards can ensure coaches have the necessary capabilities, equipment meets safety requirements and facilities are properly maintained.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But whilst raising standards, we must also ensure we don't inadvertently increase burdens, especially for small sports organisations, community clubs and grassroots coaches.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They are often important entry points for children, elderly people and beginners to access sports, and are an indispensable part of the sports ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: True team spirit means giving everyone opportunities, not leaving people behind.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When establishing standards, listening widely to opinions and ensuring standards are appropriate can promote the healthy development of the entire sports ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Fourth, the amendment further strengthens the institutional foundation for athlete development.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Athlete development requires systematic cultivation and stable support, including connections between school, community and national-level training systems.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The revision allows the Council to more clearly support training institutions, and makes different training pathways smoother, giving more young people with potential opportunities for continued development.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Fifth, we must also face the resource allocation challenges we may encounter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As sporting forms continue to increase, demand for facilities, programmes and coaching resources will also rise accordingly.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Facing these potential challenges, I propose three suggestions: First, establish a clear outcome-oriented resource framework, prioritising resources in areas that can bring the greatest social benefits.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When resources are limited, we must ensure every investment produces maximum public value.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Schools, community clubs, sports institutions and businesses have different resources and venues.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If we can better share and coordinate, we can benefit more residents without significantly increasing budgets.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When resources can be shared, sports can go further and reach more people.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, conduct "precision expansion" for programmes that show obvious growth and have long-term benefits for public health.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, family fitness activities, mind sports and some rapidly growing new programmes can start with small-scale pilots, then gradually expand based on effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Resource expansion cannot be blind, but requires precise and detailed planning, ensuring every new investment truly benefits more Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, I would like to propose three considerations for the Government in long-term sports resource planning: First, as programmes continue to increase, how should resource allocation be based on a national outcomes framework to avoid weakening support for existing community sports?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Second, if sporting demand continues to rise, will the Government appropriately expand resources based on long-term public health goals, rather than just redistributing within existing resources?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, when establishing new standards, how can we ensure standards are reasonable and would not burden small organisations excessively, excluding them from the sports ecosystem?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Gymnastics training taught me that step by step, with continuous effort, we can create real change.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This amendment may not immediately produce champions, but it can help more Singaporeans become healthier, happier and more confident in the sporting ecosystem we are building.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, this Bill strengthens our national sports framework, making it more comprehensive and future-ready.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It better reflects our Singaporeans of all ages' participation in sports and physical activity today.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As a former national gymnast, I experienced firsthand how sports build not just physical skill, but discipline, focus, resiliency and sportsmanship.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These values stayed with me for life and continue to shape who I am today.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Whether in community clubs, parks or schools, sport builds energy, inclusion and a shared sense of purpose across age and background.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Key enhancements in the Bill: one, updating the definition of "sports".

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These activities, like traditional sports, require strategy, focus, endurance and teamwork.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Including them allows for better governance and support, ensuring healthy and responsible development while recognising changing participation patterns.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Activities, such as yoga, fitness training, aerobics and running, are increasingly popular and contribute significantly to physical and mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Including these activities affirms their public value and provides a clearer framework to promote active lifestyles across communities.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, standards must be proportionate and inclusive, so that small sports organisations, community clubs and grassroots coaches are not overburdened or, worse, excluded.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Athlete development requires coordinated and sustained support, from schools to community, then to national systems.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The amendments provide clearer institutional support for training providers and smoother pathways for young athletes to develop their potential.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: There are also some long-term considerations that we need to take note.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: One, how resource allocation can expand without weakening existing community sports.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Two, whether resources should grow in line with long-term public health goals or not just reallocated.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Three, how new standards can be set without imposing excessive burdens on smaller organisations.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As in any sports, progress comes step by step, through consistent effort.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill may not immediately produce champions tomorrow, but it will help more Singaporeans become healthier, happier and more confident.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill will also enhance our current system and framework to support and boost the performance standards for our athletes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I will focus on four aspects: first, supporting active ageing through mind sports; second, engaging youths through e-sports; third, professionalising sport as a career; and last, expanding flexible sports spaces while managing residents' needs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, engaging our seniors through active ageing and mind sports.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore's rapidly ageing population requires innovative approaches to keep our seniors active, engaged and cognitively healthy.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As SportSG continues to expand physical fitness activities under ActiveSG programming, how will the Ministry ensure that the needs and aspirations of our increasing number of seniors are sufficiently catered for?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I commend the great work on offering free workout classes in the community, including many senior-friendly classes, such as "Gold" Zumba or the "Lite" version of KpopX, which are very well-received by my residents.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that the funding for this will continue in the long term as it has gotten many seniors to remain active and form social bonds.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This Bill recognises mind sports, such as chess, bridge, weiqi and xiangqi, which are very much enjoyed by both our young and our seniors.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mind sports provide participants with intellectual stimulation and social interaction.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They are activities that all can enjoy and have fun playing, regardless of age or physical abilities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This accessibility is transformative as it allows for greater inclusivity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unlike many physical sports that require certain fitness levels or mobility, mind sports can engage seniors competitively while delivering measurable cognitive, mental and social benefits.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For seniors, the benefits of mind sports extend beyond recreation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Research consistently shows that cognitively engaging activities, like chess, reduce the risk of Alzheimer's disease and cognitive decline.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
